Player starting a hand with 3 chips is eliminated and keeps 3 chips
Player starting a hand with exactly 4 chips stays active and plays
Deal removes one card per active player from a refilled deck
Eliminated player is not dealt a card; deck refilled and only active players draw
Two callers: pot is paid out to one of them (card chance decides which), folders lose only the ante
Ante takes 1 chip from each of 4 active players into the pot
Talk with 5 players then all fold: hand completes, pot holds 5 antes
Bet 3 then fold at call: chips 36 and pot 7 carries over
First-bet folder loses only the ante and is not asked to call
H is the highest bet: Bet 1 caller pays 2 more when the other bet 3 and folded
Caller who bet 2 against H=3 pays 1 more and wins pot of 10 alone
Bettor who folds at call step forfeits ante and bet
Two callers: pot goes to one caller and becomes 0 (winner by chance not asserted)

spec_choices.why: Kept from the source and the designer. Four is the smallest table where several opponents' cards give real information about your own and where there are rivals to bluff. Above 6, each player's card information and message get lost in a long conversation.

spec_choices.what: Talk kept as a simultaneous poll broadcast to all
spec_choices.why: The rules require simultaneous messages. Talk earns its place: each player knows facts the others need (their cards) and has reason to lie about them, so following a claim can cost chips.

spec_choices.what: Card strength encoded as a number from 1 to 52 (rank_index*4 + suit_index)
spec_choices.why: This lets the showdown winner be found by arithmetic (the highest card_value among callers) and exactly matches the rank-then-suit order in the rules.

spec_choices.what: Eligibility check and early-end check placed at the start of each round, with a further end check after the showdown
spec_choices.why: Elimination happens at the start of a hand. Checking right after it stops a hand being played with a single active player.

A thoughtful player infers their own card from the others' cards, their messages and their bets, and decides when to bluff, mislead others about their cards, or fold cheaply. A thoughtless player bets blindly.

simplifications.what: Shuffling the full deck each hand is done by resetting the deck list to 52 cards and drawing at random
simplifications.why: The engine has no shuffle; drawing at random from a full list is equivalent.

simplifications.what: The discarded leftover pot is simply ignored at the end
simplifications.why: It does not affect anyone's chips or the ranking.

variation.original_summary: Indian Poker (Blind Man's Bluff) deals each of 4 to 10 players one card that they hold to their forehead, so each player sees every card but their own. One round of poker betting in turn order follows, and the highest card among players who did not fold wins the pot.

review.evidence: Folding, calling and raising do change the outcome, and no single action is always best. But betting goes in turn order, so the last seat to act sees everyone else's bets before deciding, which is a built-in positional edge in a single hand. 'Always fold' only ever loses the ante, which is safe but losing. Nothing structurally breaks the game.

The original is one hand with one card each. Who holds the highest card decides it almost entirely. A brilliant reader of other players still loses when dealt a 3, and a thoughtless caller wins when dealt an ace.

There is real depth: you infer your own card from the cards you see and from how others bet against you. But a single hand gives no room for a strong player's edge to accumulate, so improvement barely shows in results.

This is the game's core strength. Your own card is the one thing hidden from you. You must estimate it from the distribution of the cards you see and from how opponents, who can see your card, choose to bet. That is classic opponent modelling and inference from limited information.
The winner is the highest card among players who stayed in (suits break ties), and chip movements are arithmetic. No judge is needed.

Hidden cards, private views and numeric bets are all supported. However, open-ended poker betting (check, bet, raise and re-raise in turn order until everyone has matched) is a loop of unknown length, which the flat step list cannot express. A single hand is also too short to score meaningfully.

problems: A single hand makes the result almost pure card luck; skill cannot show.
Open-ended sequential betting (raise and re-raise until matched) is an unbounded loop the engine cannot build.
Turn-order betting gives a fixed positional edge to whoever acts last.
There is no multi-round planning: no chip management, no reputation, nothing carried between decisions.
Folding costs only the ante, so very tight play is cheap and the game can stall into everyone folding.
The table-talk and bluffing that make the game fun in person are informal, so a text platform has no defined channel for them.

changes.what: Play a match of 16 hands, with chips carried from hand to hand. The winner is the player with the most chips at the end.
changes.why: Card luck evens out over 16 hands, while good reading, folding and bluffing accumulate. Chip management and reputation across hands add planning.
changes.fixes: A single hand makes the result almost pure card luck; skill cannot show.

changes.what: Replace open betting with two fixed simultaneous decisions. First, everyone at the same moment chooses Fold or a bet of 1, 2 or 3 chips. Then the bets are revealed, and every remaining player at the same moment chooses Call (match the highest bet) or Fold.
changes.why: This keeps the bet, see and respond structure of poker in a fixed number of steps the engine can build.
changes.fixes: Open-ended sequential betting (raise and re-raise until matched) is an unbounded loop the engine cannot build.

changes.why: No seat ever acts with more information than another, so position gives no edge.
changes.fixes: Turn-order betting gives a fixed positional edge to whoever acts last.

changes.what: If every player folds, or nobody is left to contest the pot, the whole pot carries over to the next hand.
changes.why: Mass folding feeds a bigger future pot, which raises the stakes and punishes passive play relative to opponents who contest it.
changes.fixes: Folding costs only the ante, so very tight play is cheap and the game can stall into everyone folding.

changes.what: Before betting each hand, every player writes one short public message at the same moment, and all messages are then shown. Players may say anything, including true or false claims about other players' cards.
changes.why: This formalises Indian Poker's table talk. You can try to scare a strong player out or lure a weak one in, but the other players see that player's card and know whether you lied. That rewards bluffing, reading and tracking reputation.
changes.fixes: The table-talk and bluffing that make the game fun in person are informal, so a text platform has no defined channel for them.

changes.what: Use a fixed ante, a bet cap of 3 chips and 40 starting chips. A player who has fewer than 4 chips at the start of a hand is eliminated and keeps that total.
changes.why: Losses per hand are bounded, so chip management across the match matters and one hand cannot decide everything.
changes.fixes: There is no multi-round planning: no chip management, no reputation, nothing carried between decisions.

keeps: Each player sees every card except their own.
You infer your own card from what you see and from how others bet against you.
Ante, bet, call or fold, then a showdown where the highest card among those still in wins the pot.
A standard 52-card deck, with suits breaking ties in the order Spades, Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs.
Table talk and bluffing as part of play.

recommendation.reason: The core (you are the only one blind to your own card) is an excellent inference and opponent-modelling engine. It only needs a multi-hand structure, bounded simultaneous betting and a defined talk channel.

variation.name: Forehead Poker Match
variation.summary: A 16-hand Indian Poker match for 4 to 6 players. Everyone sees every card but their own. Each hand has one simultaneous public message, one simultaneous bet and one simultaneous call-or-fold decision. Chips carry over, and the most chips after 16 hands wins.
variation.rules:
SETUP: Each player starts with 40 chips. The pot starts at 0. The match lasts 16 hands.

CARD STRENGTH: A standard 52-card deck is used. Rank from high to low is A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. Between equal ranks, suit decides, from high to low: Spades, Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs. No two cards are ever equal.

EACH HAND:
1. ELIGIBILITY: Any active player with fewer than 4 chips is eliminated. They take no further part, and their current chips are their final total.
2. DEAL: The full deck is shuffled and one card is dealt to each active player. Each player is privately told the card of every other active player, but never their own.
3. ANTE: Each active player pays 1 chip into the pot.
4. TALK: Every active player writes one short message (at most 40 words) at the same moment, without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages may say anything, including claims about anyone's card, and none of them binds anyone.
5. FIRST BET: Every active player, at the same moment, chooses one option: Fold, Bet 1, Bet 2 or Bet 3. A player who bets pays that many chips into the pot immediately. A player who folds is out of this hand and has lost only the ante.
6. REVEAL BETS: Every player's choice from step 5 is shown to everyone. Let H be the highest bet made.
7. CALL OR FOLD: Every player who bet in step 5, at the same moment, chooses Call or Fold. Calling costs H minus that player's own step-5 bet, paid into the pot. A player whose bet was already H calls for free. Folding forfeits everything that player has put in this hand.
8. SHOWDOWN: Find the players who called.
   - Two or more callers: their cards are compared, and the caller with the strongest card wins the whole pot.
   - Exactly one caller: that player wins the whole pot without comparison.
   - No callers: the pot stays and carries over to the next hand.
   All cards are then revealed to everyone, so players can check what was said and bet.
9. Winnings are added to the winner's chips, the pot resets to 0 (unless it carried over), and the next hand begins.

END: The match ends after hand 16, or earlier if only one player is still active. Any pot remaining at that moment is discarded.
variation.objective: The player with the most chips at the end of the match wins. Eliminated players count with the chips they held when eliminated. If two or more players tie for the most chips, the game is a draw among them.
variation.expected_effect:
The game becomes a contest of reading your own invisible card. A player infers their card's strength from the cards they can see (if everyone else holds low cards, yours is probably higher) and from how others bet and talk, since every opponent can see your card exactly.

Simple policies lose:
- Always Fold loses 1 chip per hand and finishes about 16 chips down.
- Always Bet 3 and Call is exploited. Opponents see its card, so they fold when it is high (it wins only the antes) and call when it is low (it loses 4 chips each time).
- Always Bet 1 and Call never pressures anyone and pays to see every losing showdown.
- Random play bleeds chips to anyone who folds when they see the table is strong.

When everyone plays well, card luck still swings individual hands, but over 16 hands the player who folds weak cards cheaply, extracts value with strong ones and bluffs effectively finishes ahead.

Talk passes both tests. On reasoning, players can bluff and bait, for example telling a player holding the 2 'you look strong' to lure them into calling, or telling the player holding the ace 'there is a king out there' to scare them off. Each listener must weigh who gains from the claim and that speaker's past honesty, which can be checked because cards are revealed after each hand. On conflict, only one player can win and every pot is zero-sum, so following another player's advice about your own card is exactly how a credulous player loses: the speaker only says 'call' when your call pays them.

No seat has an edge because all choices are simultaneous. The carry-over pot stops everyone from folding into a stall.

balanced.evidence:
STRUCTURE: Every choice is a simultaneous poll and every player sees exactly N-1 cards, all but their own. No seat has a move-order or information edge. The game is zero-sum in chips, apart from a carried pot that is discarded at the end.

MAIN DECISION (4 players, cards numbered 1-52 by strength): a player who sees a highest visible card m has a chance of holding a better card equal to (52-m minus visible cards above m)/49.
- Highest visible 10C (m=33): 19/49 = 39%.
- Highest visible KS (m=52-4=48): 4/49 = 8%.
- Highest visible 6C (m=17): 35/49 = 71%.
So the right action depends on what you see and on what the others bet. No action is right everywhere.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the WINNER RULE (most chips wins):
(a) Always Fold (first option): loses the 1-chip ante every hand, 16 chips over 16 hands, and ends on 24. The other N-1 players share the +16, so their average is about 40+16/(N-1) (≥43.2 at N=6). Always Fold wins 0 hands and loses or finishes last essentially every match. FAILS as a policy.
(b) Always Bet 3 and Call (highest bet): costs 4 per hand. Sensible opponents see its card. They call when that card is weak and fold when it is strong. Approximate payoff at N=4: when its card is strongest (about 25%) it mostly wins only antes plus its own bet back, a net gain of about +3. Otherwise it usually meets a better caller and loses 4. EV ≈ 0.25×3 − 0.75×4 = −2.25 per hand, about −36 over 16 hands. It is likely eliminated (fewer than 4 chips) before hand 16. Against random players EV is about 0 with high variance, and it is not near-always winning.
(c) Always Bet 1 and Call: it reaches the same commitment H as (b) but sets lower stakes. It is exploited the same way by players who raise H when they see its card is low.
(d) Always Bet 1 then decide: this is not thoughtless. It is the cheap-option line.

DOMINANCE: Bet 1 keeps a cheaper fold option, so it is not dominated. Bet 3 is not dominated either, because only a high bet raises H and makes rivals pay up to 2 more to call. Neither is strictly better.

NEVER-LOSES CHECK: No policy is immune to losing. A folder loses the ante every hand, and any caller can be beaten at showdown. There is no cooperative structure that a safe option could undercut. All N players can realistically win.

LABEL CHECK: The variation is described as competitive poker, and its payoffs are pure zero-sum pot transfers, which matches the description.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS:
- Every situation is defined:
  - All players fold in step 5: the pot carries over.
  - A lone bettor equals H, calls free and wins.
  - Several callers: the strongest card wins.
  - No callers: the pot carries.
- Card order is total because suits break ties.
- Elimination below 4 chips guarantees every active player can afford the maximum outlay of 1+3=4.
- Ending and tie (draw) rules are explicit, and the leftover pot is discarded.
- The winner is decided by chip arithmetic.

FINITE: at most 16 hands.

LIMITS:
- steps 16 ≤ 20
- choice steps 3 (talk, bet, call) ≤ 4
- attributes 10 ≤ 20
- hidden elements 1 ≤ 3
- random draws 1 ≤ 1
- rounds 16 ≤ 40

ENGINE FIT:
- Seeing others' cards but not your own uses private_values/private_channel.
- The deck uses the shared_deck_draw workaround.
- Comparing cards is a numeric max on card values held in table attributes.
- elimination and fixed_rounds are supported.
- No board, clock, trading or binding agreement is needed.

TALK: The game has 4-6 players with opposed interests, and each player holds information the others lack (their cards). Talk is meaningful here. A player can truthfully or falsely tell C that C's card is low to make C fold, and listeners must weigh each speaker's incentive. Following a claim can cost you the pot. Talk is simultaneous (all write, then all are shown), as required.

LATE ROUNDS: This is not a cooperation game, so there is no betrayal dynamic. In late hands a leader may choose to fold and pay only antes, which is a legitimate strategic tradeoff, not a degenerate safe-option win. A large enough lead is needed, and chasers can still raise stakes against them.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT TO INFER: Each player must estimate their own hidden card from three sources:
1. The N-1 visible cards (the probability table above).
2. The simultaneous talk claims, which are possibly lies, and their senders' incentives.
3. The revealed step-5 bets, because opponents bet on how your card compares with theirs.
The step-7 call decision acts on all of this.

PLANNING AND MODELLING:
- Opponents' bet patterns and honesty are revealed at each showdown (all cards are shown), so reputations form over 16 hands.
- Chip-stack management matters: the elimination threshold, folding to protect a lead, and raising H to pressure short stacks.

CHANCE: Each hand's card is random, but 16 independent deals average out. A good player limits losses on weak cards by folding (losing 1 instead of 4) and extracts more when strong. A bad deal can be overcome. The skill swing is roughly 3 chips per hand in folding decisions alone. My estimate is that about 35-45% of the outcome between equally skilled players comes from the deal, and much less between unequal players.

ALL-GOOD MIRROR: With identical good strategies the winner varies with the deal sequence. This is ordinary card-game variance spread over 16 independent deals, not a single hidden type deciding everything. A player who reasons well, for example avoiding calls when the visible max is high or reading bluffs, is clearly favoured over one who does not.

triage.reason: In every failing scenario the game's chips and pot are correct for the moves it actually received. In the Bet 3 case seat 1 bet 3, everyone else folded and seat 1 called, so as sole caller it rightly won the 7-chip pot and ended on 43. The tests expected the state you would get if the bettor had folded at the call step (36 chips, pot 7 carried over), but they never scripted that fold; they relied on the 'decline' default and on the hand stopping halfway.
triage.guidance: A one-round scenario plays the whole hand: ante, bets, call step, showdown and payout. Write expectations for the state after payout. For every scenario that depends on a call-step choice, script that choice explicitly ('Call' or 'Fold') for each bettor rather than relying on the default. For the Bet 3 test, either script seat 1 to Fold at the call step and expect 36 chips and pot 7 carried over, or keep the Call and expect 43 chips and pot 0. For the 'bettor folds at call step' and 'only bettor folds, pot carries over' tests, give the folding seat an explicit 'Fold' rule at the call step. For 'caller who bet H pays nothing more', script both players' bets and calls, then work out the payout to the stronger card from the dealt card values for that seed, or use a setup where the winner does not depend on chance. Do not assert on mid-hand values that the showdown changes later in the same round.
